newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy insurer RAS has paid some Holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: Italy insurer RAS has paid some Holocaust claims.

text.p: Italian insurance company Riunione Adriatica di Sicurta (RAS) said it has compensated a number of descendants of Holocaust victims who held policies issued by the company in Eastern Europe before World War Two.

A spokesman for the company in Milan said on Wednesday that RAS had received 30 life insurance claims over the past five years. "In nine cases we have given a symbolic contribution in the form of free life insurance policies of short duration," the spokesman said.
RAS is part of Germany's Allianz group.
RAS operated a network of subsidiaries throughout Eastern Europe before the war but the companies were siezed by communist governments in the 1940s and all records of policy-holders were lost.

"The big problem is that we do not have any archives from these companies," the spokesman said. "We examined each of the requests on the basis of documentation presented by individual claimants," he added.
The spokesman declined to put a value on the new policies issued to descendants of Holocaust victims or to say who they were.

RAS had not yet been formally notified of a suit filed in New York by Holocaust victims and their families alleging a group of European insurance companies including RAS and another Italian insurer, Generali, withheld, concealed or converted the proceeds of policies sold before 1946.
A spokesman for Generali also said the company, based in Trieste, was awaiting formal notification of the suit filed on Monday with a Manhattan federal court.
Generali said last month that reports that it could be liable for tens of thousands of life insurance claims from descendants of Holocaust victims were without foundation.
The company also said it was ready to throw open its records at its headquarters in the Northeastern port city of Trieste but it was not willing to recognise any legal liability.

Generali said all its businesses in Eastern Europe were expropriated after the war by communist governments and policies issued by them no longer were legal obligations of Generali but of the governments which carried out the nationalisations.
Generali had a dominant share of the insurance market in Eastern Europe before the war.
In Israel, Generali has been given the go-ahead to make a tender offer for shares in local insurer Leumi Insurance Holdings it does not already own.
Some Israeli legislators are campaigning for Generali to compensate families of policy-holders who perished in the Holocaust.
